The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: Shop requests responded far more slowly than usual
Why, in plain words: The shop's automatic scaling likely kept taking away the extra servers it had just added, because a setting meant to make it wait before scaling back down was set to zero, and that left too few servers to answer requests quickly.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 8m 43s {duration}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop - confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #544 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
Shop requests responded far more slowly than usual
Incident: HighLatency on io-shop
Date: Nov 11, 2026, 03:15 to 03:23:43 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 6 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 11, 2026, 03:43:27 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 11, 2026, 03:23:16 UTC
Ended by: Argus: raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop - confirmed, still in place

Summary
The service broke at 03:15 UTC and was back to normal at 03:23:43 UTC, 8 minutes 43 seconds later. What its alert watches went from 215 ms before it began to 1811 ms at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. The shop's automatic scaling likely kept taking away the extra servers it had just added, because a setting meant to make it wait before scaling back down was set to zero, and that left too few servers to answer requests quickly. What Argus did: raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop (can be put back) - confirmed, still in place. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #544, for a person to review and merge. Argus left automatic sync of io-shop off, to be turned back on once its repository says what should run (AI-3). While the scale-down window in the shop's configuration stays at zero, the autoscaler could again drop the shop back to too few replicas as soon as its floor is lowered, and responses could slow again.

Impact
8m 43s - onset until back to normal
0.9% to 1.4% - error rate, before onset and while broken on average (no rise)
215 ms to 1034 ms - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 1811 ms; the rule's line is 600 ms)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
The production values for io-shop's HorizontalPodAutoscaler set its scale-down stabilization window to 0 seconds. As Code-Fix reads it, after scaling up from 3 to 6 replicas, the controller acted straight away on the lower per-replica CPU that its own scale-up had produced. It scaled back to 3 replicas, where CPU was pinned again, so serving capacity kept flipping up and down instead of holding. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
Causal chain
symptom People using the shop got much slower responses: its slowest requests took far longer than usual, while failed requests stayed within their normal variation.
  Evidence:
    AL1 p95 latency above threshold for 5m
    T5 03:23:33 Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 03:15
why 1 Responses slowed because io-shop had too little serving capacity for the requests coming in.
  Evidence:
    T15 03:26:12 Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 03:23
    T16 03:26:12 Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
    T17 03:26:12 Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - raised io-shop's autoscaler floor from 3 replicas to 6 and the rule that fired stopped firing
why 2 It had too little capacity because the autoscaler did not hold the higher replica count. It kept taking the service back down to its floor of 3 replicas, the count read at 03:23:33 UTC.
  Evidence:
    T6 03:23:33 Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
    T17
    F1 What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its fix
  Ruled out:
    A deploy, release or flag change on the service: the Investigator Agent asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 03:16; the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes.
      T7
      T8
    A flag change by anyone but Argus: Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:23:37.
      T11
why 3 The autoscaler scaled back down straight away because the production values set its scale-down stabilization window to 0 seconds. That let it act on the low per-replica CPU that its own scale-up had produced.
  Evidence:
    F1
Contributing factors
- No check was seen that would have stopped a production autoscaler configuration with a scale-down stabilization window of zero from going out. (AI-4)
- No alert was seen on the autoscaler repeatedly scaling io-shop up and back down. The fault was found only by the latency alert. (AI-5)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | Capacity will not settle: cpu_limit_cores flips between 3.0 and 6.0 from 03:11 UTC onward while traffic climbs. In the minutes served at 3.0 cores, CPU is pinned at the limit and p95 jumps to 1.3-1.8s. In the minutes served at 6.0 cores, p95 returns to about 212ms. Nothing was deployed. | 0.60 | confirmed
C2 | Request volume rose from 1200 to 5400 req/min starting 03:10 UTC. This outgrew the 3-core allocation, so CPU saturated and requests queued, pushing p95 up. | 0.30 | confirmed, as tested for C1

Trigger
C1 was confirmed; it blames io-shop itself and names no change to it.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 03:23:43 | Raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop for C1 | Argus | can be put back | confirmed, still in place - automatic sync left off
 | 03:28:13 | Proposed a fix: PR #544 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 03:15 UTC. HighLatency fired at 03:22:54 UTC, 7 minutes 54 seconds later.
What the alert said
AL1 | p95 latency above threshold for 5m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #544 | open
AI-3 | Turn automatic sync of io-shop back on once its repository says what should run - until then nothing merged reaches it, and turned on sooner it puts back what the repository says, undoing what Argus changed by hand | mitigate | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Add a CI check that rejects production autoscaler values with a scale-down stabilization window of zero, or below an agreed minimum, for every service. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Add an alert that fires when a service's autoscaler keeps reversing its replica count within a short window. | detect | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Link io-shop's HighLatency alert to the on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires. | process | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came 6 minutes 54 seconds after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
- 43 seconds after the alert was raised, Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:23:37.
- 49 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop for C1.
- 42 seconds after the alert was raised, the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes.
- 5 minutes 19 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #544.
What went wrong
- The alert fired on the production shop, but no on-call incident was linked to it, so nobody was paged.
Where it got lucky
Nothing.

Timeline (UTC)
 | Nov 11 03:15 | IMPACT BEGINS | the incident began
 | 03:22:54 | DETECTED | HighLatency on io-shop fired
T1 | 03:23:15 |  | Argus Received HighLatency on io-shop
T2 | 03:23:19 |  | Argus Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
T3 | 03:23:27 |  | Investigator Agent Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 03:22:54
T4 | 03:23:32 |  | Investigator Agent Read back 361 minutes of metrics
T5 | 03:23:33 |  | Investigator Agent Placed the start of the incident at 03:15
T6 | 03:23:33 |  | Investigator Agent Recorded where the 3 replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
T7 | 03:23:35 |  | Investigator Agent Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 03:16
T8 | 03:23:36 |  | Investigator Agent Read back 0 production changes
T9 | 03:23:37 |  | Investigator Agent Formed 2 candidate causes, best first: C1, C2
T10 | 03:23:37 |  | Investigator Agent Did not read logs
T11 | 03:23:37 |  | Argus Read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 03:23:37
T12 | 03:23:41 |  | Argus Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
T13 | 03:23:43 | MITIGATION APPLIED | Mitigation Agent Raised the autoscaler floor of io-shop for C1
 | 03:23:43 | IMPACT ENDS | the service was back to normal
T14 | 03:23:50 |  | Mitigation Agent Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 03:24 - up to 196s
T15 | 03:26:12 |  | Mitigation Agent Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 03:23
T16 | 03:26:12 |  | Mitigation Agent Judged the action CONFIRMED
T17 | 03:26:12 |  | Argus Moved the incident to MITIGATED - raised io-shop's autoscaler floor from 3 replicas to 6 and the rule that fired stopped firing
T18 | 03:28:13 |  | Code-Fix Agent Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #544

Response effort
none - engineer time
120,739 - tokens spent by Argus

Supporting information
The incident's walk: http://localhost:8000/incidents/09299391-fb45-4397-9175-f361934eca17
The fix it proposed: PR #544 (https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/544) opened as a draft. The record holds nothing about it after that.
Changes to production read
Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)
Not read.
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its fix
F1 | deploy/values-production.yaml renders the shop's HorizontalPodAutoscaler with minReplicas 3, maxReplicas 6, targetCpuPercent 70 and scaleDownStabilizationSeconds 0. The file's own comment says what that window is for: Kubernetes defaults it to 300 seconds, so the controller acts on the highest recommendation from the last five minutes. Otherwise it acts on a reading that its own last action produced.

At 0 the loop flaps. At 3 replicas CPU is pinned, so the controller scales to 6. At 6 replicas the per-replica CPU falls below target, and with no window the controller scales straight back to 3 on that reading, which pins CPU again. That fits the capacity the investigation saw moving between 3.0 and 6.0 cores. The 6-to-3 flip is one minute after a scale-up, while traffic is still climbing.

This change sets scaleDownStabilizationSeconds to 300, the Kubernetes default. Scale-up is unchanged and happens as soon as it is needed. Scale-down now only happens once the higher recommendation has held for five minutes, so the post-scale-up dip can no longer undo the scale-up.

Nothing under src/ reads the autoscaling block (a search for scaleDownStabilization matches only this file), so no service code or tests need to change. There is no test because the fix is in deployment configuration, not code this repository's tests exercise.
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-10
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

Review checklist
✓ Key incident data collected (met)
✓ Impact assessed (met)
○ Root-cause analysis complete (for a person)
  the proposed fix (AI-2) brings no test that would confirm the reading
○ Every action item owned and dated (for a person)
○ Reviewed and shared (for a person)

The document, by field:
overview: For {duration}, the io-shop online shop responded to requests far more slowly than usual. The likely cause was the shop's automatic scaling repeatedly taking away extra servers it had just added. A setting meant to make it wait before scaling back down was set so that it did not wait, which left too few servers to answer requests quickly. Argus estimates the cost to the shop in lost takings at {customer_loss}. Nobody was paged, so no on-call staff were called out. To end the slowdown, Argus raised the minimum number of servers the shop keeps running. That change is confirmed and still in place, and automatic syncing of the shop's settings has been left switched off. Argus has also proposed a fix, which is open as a draft and has not been applied.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
